questions.q: Why does DNS stop being a single-server afterthought once an organization has more than one VNet or VPC?
options: Azure and AWS both disable private name resolution entirely once a second VNet or VPC exists
A single network's built-in resolution doesn't help a workload in one network resolve a name in another, or resolve on-premises names during a hybrid migration
DNS only matters for public-facing websites, never for private internal resources
Every VNet or VPC is required to use the exact same private DNS zone name
questions.explain: A single network can resolve its own names fine, but a second network, or a hybrid on-premises link, introduces cross-network and cross-boundary resolution that basic per-network DNS doesn't solve.

questions.q: What does a virtual network link actually do for an Azure private DNS zone?
options: It connects the zone to a VNet so that VNet can resolve the zone's records, and it can cross subscription boundaries
It deletes the zone after 90 days if no VNet uses it
It converts a private DNS zone into a public DNS zone automatically
It is only required for on-premises DNS servers, never for Azure VNets
questions.explain: A private DNS zone only resolves for VNets it's linked to via a virtual network link, and that link can connect zones and VNets that live in different subscriptions.

questions.q: What problem does the Azure Private DNS Resolver solve that a private DNS zone alone does not?
options: It replaces the need for virtual network links entirely
It is required before any private DNS zone can be created
Hybrid resolution in both directions: inbound endpoints let on-premises query Azure private zones, and outbound endpoints forward specific domains to on-premises DNS
It only works for public DNS zones, not private ones
questions.explain: Private DNS zones alone only resolve Azure-native names for linked VNets; the Private DNS Resolver's inbound and outbound endpoints bridge Azure and on-premises DNS in both directions.

questions.q: How does an AWS Route 53 Private Hosted Zone created in one account get associated with a VPC in a different account?
options: By authorizing the association first, through Route 53's cross-account authorization API — the same cross-account sharing idea as Azure's cross-subscription virtual network link
Private Hosted Zones can never be associated across AWS accounts under any circumstance
By making the hosted zone public first, then converting it back to private
By manually copying every DNS record into the second account's own hosted zone
questions.explain: A hosted zone in one account can be associated with a VPC in another account by authorizing that association first, mirroring Azure's cross-subscription virtual network link capability.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff of centralizing DNS zones and resolver configuration in the hub rather than letting each spoke run its own?
options: Centralized DNS is technically impossible on both Azure and AWS
Centralized DNS requires every spoke to use an identical IP address range
Centralized DNS gives consistent, centrally managed resolution to every spoke, but a team wanting a nonstandard configuration has to go through the central team rather than self-serve
Centralized DNS removes the need for any hybrid connectivity to on-premises
questions.explain: Centralizing DNS avoids N inconsistent per-spoke configurations and gives one consistent policy, at the cost of spokes no longer being able to freely configure unusual DNS setups on their own.
